docs.title: European Network for Long-term Insights on Grid prices, Hedging & Trends
docs.text: ENLIGHT is a multi-year electricity market forecast model that simulates market clearing across European bidding zones using solver-based optimization.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Models all European bidding zones with multi-year foresight
  • Reproduces market clearing via optimization (Gurobi or HiGHS)
  • Scenario configuration via YAML files
  • Rolling-horizon or full-year simulation modes
  • Outputs: prices, dispatch, line flows, curtailment

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Each simulation run follows a four-step pipeline:

  1. Data Preprocessing — transforms raw input data into model-ready formats and saves to simulations/<name>/data/
  2. Data Loading — loads preprocessed data into structured objects (DataFrames, arrays)
  3. Model Execution — solves the market clearing optimization (maximise social welfare subject to power balance, generation limits, transmission capacity, storage dynamics)
  4. Results Export — extracts solutions, calculates metrics, saves to simulations/<name>/results/

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
simulations/<name>/
├── data/        # preprocessed inputs
└── results/
    ├── electricity_prices.csv
    ├── generation_schedules.csv
    ├── lineflows.csv
    ├── demand_served.csv
    └── curtailment.csv

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
ENLIGHT uses Hydra for configuration. Settings are split into two layers:

File Purpose configs/default_config.yaml Global settings: solver, bidding zones, paths configs/simulations/<name>.yaml Per-simulation settings: run mode, years, technology parameters

docs.title: Solver
docs.text: solver_name: highs   # highs (open-source) | gurobi (requires license)

docs.title: Bidding Zones
docs.text:
Uncomment zones to include them. Each active zone must have corresponding input data.

bidding_zones:
  - AT   # Austria
  - FR   # France
  # - DE  # (commented out = excluded)

docs.title: Multi-run Mode
docs.text:
Uncomment the hydra block to enable sweeps across multiple simulation configs:

hydra:
  mode: MULTIRUN
  sweeper:
    params:
      simulations: glob(*)

docs.title: Run Control
docs.text:
run:
  mode:              rolling_horizon   # rolling_horizon | yearly
  prediction_year:   2040              # capacity/demand projection year
  plant_aggregation: true              # aggregate units by zone+fuel

rolling_horizon:
  start_week: 1    # [1-52]
  end_week:   52   # [1-52]

docs.title: Production Technologies
docs.text:
Each technology block follows the same pattern:

wind_onshore:
  weather_year:  2020                      # historical profile year
  capacity_file: TYNDP_2024_National_Trends
  bid_price:     0.01                      # EUR/MWh

Technologies: wind_onshore, wind_offshore, solar_pv, hydro_ror, hydro_res, hydro_ps, thermal.

docs.title: Demand
docs.text:
Demand is split into inflexible (price-inelastic, bid at voll) and flexible (price-elastic, bid at wtp) categories.

Categories within each: classical, industrial, household, public, ev.

demand_inflexible:
  classical:
    profile_year: 2020
    amount_file:  TYNDP_2024_National_Trends
    voll:         5000   # EUR/MWh — value of lost load

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
bess:
  units_file:           bess_units
  initial_soc:          0.5    # fraction of capacity at t=0
  roundtrip_efficiency: 0.85

docs.title: Running with Docker (Gurobi)
docs.text: Some Gurobi licenses restrict usage to machines with 8 or fewer CPU cores. If your machine has more, the solver will refuse to run. The Docker setup in dockerfiles/ works around this by running the solver inside a container capped at 7 CPUs, which satisfies the license check regardless of the host hardware.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker Desktop installed and running
  • A valid gurobi.lic license file

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. Place your license file somewhere stable on your machine, for example:

~/.gurobi/gurobi.lic

2. Set the environment variable so Docker knows where to find it:

# Linux / macOS
export GRB_LICENSE_FILE=~/.gurobi/gurobi.lic

# Windows (PowerShell)
$env:GRB_LICENSE_FILE = "$HOME\.gurobi\gurobi.lic"

You can add this line to your shell profile (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc) to avoid repeating it.

3. Build the image from the repo root:

docker compose -f dockerfiles/docker-compose.gurobi.yml build

This installs all Python dependencies and the Gurobi solver inside the image. The license file is never copied into the image.

docs.title: Running a simulation
docs.text:
docker compose -f dockerfiles/docker-compose.gurobi.yml run gurobi

Pass Hydra overrides as you normally would:

docker compose -f dockerfiles/docker-compose.gurobi.yml run gurobi simulations=sim_1
docker compose -f dockerfiles/docker-compose.gurobi.yml run gurobi --multirun simulations=sim_1,sim_2

Results are written to outputs/ in your local repo, exactly as when running without Docker.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
You edit code and configs in your local repo as usual. The container is only invoked for the solve step. Git works normally throughout.

edit code / configs locally
        |
        v
docker compose ... run gurobi simulations=sim_1
        |
        v
outputs/ appears in your local repo
        |
        v
git add / commit / push as usual

docs.title: Rebuilding the image
docs.text:
Rebuild only when pyproject.toml or uv.lock changes (i.e. when dependencies change). Config and data changes do not require a rebuild because configs/ and data/ are mounted as volumes.

docker compose -f dockerfiles/docker-compose.gurobi.yml build --no-cache

docs.title: Gurobi version
docs.text:
The image uses gurobi/python:13.0.1_3.12 by default. To use a different version, edit the GUROBI_VERSION build arg in dockerfiles/docker-compose.gurobi.yml or pass it at build time:

docker compose -f dockerfiles/docker-compose.gurobi.yml build --build-arg GUROBI_VERSION=12.0.2

Available tags are listed on the Gurobi Docker Hub page.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python >= 3.12
  • A valid Gurobi license (optional — HiGHS is the open-source alternative)
  • An ENTSO-E API key (optional — required for live data fetching)

docs.title: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/marco-saretta-DTU/enlight.git
cd enlight

docs.title: Install with uv (recommended)
docs.text:
uv sync          # creates .venv and installs all dependencies
uv run main.py   # run the model

If uv is not installed:

# macOS / Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

docs.title: Install with conda
docs.text:
conda env create -f envs/environment.yaml
conda activate enlight-env
python main.py

docs.title: ENTSO-E API Key
docs.text:
Place your key in configs/entsoe_api_key/placeholder.yaml:

entsoe_api_key: "YOUR-KEY-GOES-HERE"

docs.title: 1. Pick or create a simulation config
docs.text:
Simulation configs live in configs/simulations/. Copy the template and rename it:

cp configs/simulations/_template.yaml configs/simulations/my_sim.yaml

Edit my_sim.yaml to set the run mode, prediction year, and any parameters you want to change.

docs.title: 2. Set the active simulation
docs.text:
Open configs/default_config.yaml and point the simulations default at your file:

defaults:
  - simulations: my_sim   # ← your filename without .yaml

docs.title: 3. Run
docs.text:
# Single simulation
uv run main.py

# Or explicitly select a config from the CLI
uv run main.py simulations=my_sim

docs.title: 4. Multi-run (sweep over all configs)
docs.text:
uv run main.py --multirun simulations='glob(*)'

# Or select specific configs
uv run main.py --multirun simulations=sim_1,sim_2

docs.title: 5. Find the results
docs.text:
simulations/<label>/
├── data/      # preprocessed inputs
└── results/   # prices, dispatch, flows, curtailment

The label field in your simulation config controls the output folder name.
